claim: In mouse hairy skin, lanceolate complexes are associated with three types of hair follicles: guard, awl/auchene and zigzag.
source: In mouse hairy skin, lanceolate complexes associated with three types of hair follicles, guard, awl/auchene and zigzag, serve as mechanosensory end organs.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and introduction sections of the manuscript.

claim: Lanceolate complexes serve as mechanosensory end organs.
source: In mouse hairy skin, lanceolate complexes associated with three types of hair follicles, guard, awl/auchene and zigzag, serve as mechanosensory end organs.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract about the function of lanceolate complexes.

claim: Lanceolate complexes are formed by unique combinations of low-threshold mechanoreceptors (LTMRs): Aβ RA-LTMRs, Aδ-LTMRs, and C-LTMRs.
source: These structures are formed by unique combinations of low-threshold mechanoreceptors (LTMRs), Aβ RA-LTMRs, Aδ-LTMRs, and C-LTMRs, and their associated terminal Schwann cells (TSCs).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a description of the cellular composition of lanceolate complexes.

claim: Lanceolate complexes include terminal Schwann cells (TSCs) associated with LTMR endings.
source: These structures are formed by unique combinations of low-threshold mechanoreceptors (LTMRs), Aβ RA-LTMRs, Aδ-LTMRs, and C-LTMRs, and their associated terminal Schwann cells (TSCs).
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1.

claim: TSC processes at hair follicles are tiled.
source: We found that TSC processes at hair follicles are tiled and that individual TSCs host axonal endings of more than one LTMR subtype.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through genetic labeling experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Individual TSCs host axonal endings of more than one LTMR subtype.
source: We found that TSC processes at hair follicles are tiled and that individual TSCs host axonal endings of more than one LTMR subtype.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by triple labeling experiments shown in Figure 3C,C′.

claim: Schwann cell ablation leads to loss of LTMR terminals at hair follicles.
source: Moreover, Schwann cell ablation leads to loss of LTMR terminals at hair follicles while, in contrast, TSCs remain associated with hair follicles following skin denervation in adult mice and, remarkably, become re-associated with newly formed axons, indicating a TSC-dependence of lanceolate complex maintenance and regeneration in adults.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through genetic ablation experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: TSCs remain associated with hair follicles following skin denervation in adult mice.
source: Moreover, Schwann cell ablation leads to loss of LTMR terminals at hair follicles while, in contrast, TSCs remain associated with hair follicles following skin denervation in adult mice and, remarkably, become re-associated with newly formed axons, indicating a TSC-dependence of lanceolate complex maintenance and regeneration in adults.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through denervation experiments shown in Figure 9.

claim: TSCs become re-associated with newly formed axons following denervation.
source: Moreover, Schwann cell ablation leads to loss of LTMR terminals at hair follicles while, in contrast, TSCs remain associated with hair follicles following skin denervation in adult mice and, remarkably, become re-associated with newly formed axons, indicating a TSC-dependence of lanceolate complex maintenance and regeneration in adults.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through re-innervation experiments shown in Figure 10.

claim: Lanceolate complex maintenance and regeneration in adults is TSC-dependent.
source: Moreover, Schwann cell ablation leads to loss of LTMR terminals at hair follicles while, in contrast, TSCs remain associated with hair follicles following skin denervation in adult mice and, remarkably, become re-associated with newly formed axons, indicating a TSC-dependence of lanceolate complex maintenance and regeneration in adults.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the abstract based on the experimental findings from ablation and denervation experiments.

claim: More than 90% of the body surface of most mammals is covered by hair follicles.
source: More than 90% of the body surface of most mammals is covered by hair follicles, which regulate body temperature, facilitate perspiration, and are involved in the perception of mechanosensory stimuli upon the skin.
evidence: This is a statement of general knowledge about mammalian anatomy.

claim: Hair follicles regulate body temperature.
source: More than 90% of the body surface of most mammals is covered by hair follicles, which regulate body temperature, facilitate perspiration, and are involved in the perception of mechanosensory stimuli upon the skin.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about hair follicle function.

claim: Hair follicles facilitate perspiration.
source: More than 90% of the body surface of most mammals is covered by hair follicles, which regulate body temperature, facilitate perspiration, and are involved in the perception of mechanosensory stimuli upon the skin.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about hair follicle function.

claim: Hair follicles are involved in the perception of mechanosensory stimuli upon the skin.
source: More than 90% of the body surface of most mammals is covered by hair follicles, which regulate body temperature, facilitate perspiration, and are involved in the perception of mechanosensory stimuli upon the skin.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and is the focus of the study.

claim: There are three major hair follicle subtypes in mouse back hairy skin: guard, awl/auchene, and zigzag.
source: There are three major hair follicle subtypes in mouse back hairy skin: guard, awl/auchene, and zigzag.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction and is established knowledge cited from previous work (Schlake, 2007; Driskell et al., 2009; Li et al., 2011).

claim: Guard hairs make up approximately 1% of the back skin hairs of the mouse.
source: Guard hairs, which make up ∼1% of the back skin hairs of the mouse, develop during the first wave of hair follicle morphogenesis, beginning E13–14.5.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about hair follicle composition.

claim: Guard hairs develop during the first wave of hair follicle morphogenesis, beginning E13–14.5.
source: Guard hairs, which make up ∼1% of the back skin hairs of the mouse, develop during the first wave of hair follicle morphogenesis, beginning E13–14.5.
evidence: This is stated as established developmental knowledge.

claim: Guard hairs have the longest hair shafts that have two rows of medulla cells and do not contain kinks.
source: These hairs have the longest hair shafts that have two rows of medulla cells and do not contain kinks.
evidence: This is a morphological description of guard hairs stated in the introduction.

claim: Awl hairs form during the second wave of murine hair morphogenesis, beginning E15–16.5.
source: Awl hairs, which form during the second wave of murine hair morphogenesis, beginning E15–16.5, are straight but are shorter than guard hairs and contain three or four rows of medulla cells.
evidence: This is stated as established developmental knowledge.

claim: Awl hairs are straight but are shorter than guard hairs and contain three or four rows of medulla cells.
source: Awl hairs, which form during the second wave of murine hair morphogenesis, beginning E15–16.5, are straight but are shorter than guard hairs and contain three or four rows of medulla cells.
evidence: This is a morphological description of awl hairs.

claim: Auchene hairs are developmentally and morphologically identical to awl hairs, except that they have one kink in the hair.
source: Auchene hairs are developmentally and morphologically identical to awl hairs, except that they have one kink in the hair.
evidence: This is a morphological description distinguishing auchene from awl hairs.

claim: Awl/auchene hairs together make up approximately 20% of back skin hairs.
source: Awl/auchene hairs together make up ∼20% of back skin hairs and, for the purposes of this study, are considered together.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about hair follicle composition.

claim: Zigzag hairs form during the third wave of hair morphogenesis beginning at E18.5.
source: Finally, zigzag hairs form during the third wave of hair morphogenesis beginning at E18.5 and are the most abundant type, making up ∼80% of hairs.
evidence: This is stated as established developmental knowledge.

claim: Zigzag hairs are the most abundant type, making up approximately 80% of hairs.
source: Finally, zigzag hairs form during the third wave of hair morphogenesis beginning at E18.5 and are the most abundant type, making up ∼80% of hairs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about hair follicle composition.

claim: Zigzag hairs have one row of medulla cells and at least two bends in their hair shaft.
source: Zigzag hairs have one row of medulla cells and at least two bends in their hair shaft (Schlake, 2007; Driskell et al., 2009; Li et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a morphological description of zigzag hairs with citations to previous work.

claim: Guard hair follicles are innervated by Aβ RA-LTMR lanceolate endings.
source: Indeed, guard hair follicles are innervated by Aβ RA-LTMR lanceolate endings and are also associated with Aβ SA1-LTMR Merkel endings.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by previous work (Li et al., 2011).

claim: Guard hair follicles are associated with Aβ SA1-LTMR Merkel endings.
source: Indeed, guard hair follicles are innervated by Aβ RA-LTMR lanceolate endings and are also associated with Aβ SA1-LTMR Merkel endings.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by previous work (Li et al., 2011).

claim: Awl/auchene hairs are triply innervated by inter-digitated Aβ RA-, Aδ-, and C-LTMR lanceolate endings.
source: In contrast, awl/auchene hairs are triply innervated by inter-digitated Aβ RA-, Aδ-, and C-LTMR lanceolate endings, whereas zigzag hair follicles are innervated by inter-digitated Aδ- and C-LTMR lanceolate endings (Li et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to previous work (Li et al., 2011).

claim: Zigzag hair follicles are innervated by inter-digitated Aδ- and C-LTMR lanceolate endings.
source: In contrast, awl/auchene hairs are triply innervated by inter-digitated Aβ RA-, Aδ-, and C-LTMR lanceolate endings, whereas zigzag hair follicles are innervated by inter-digitated Aδ- and C-LTMR lanceolate endings (Li et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to previous work (Li et al., 2011).

claim: C-LTMRs can be visualized in ThCreER; Rosa26LSL-tdTomato mice treated with 4-HT.
source: We found that C-LTMRs can be visualized in ThCreER; Rosa26LSL-tdTomato mice treated with 4-HT; Aδ-LTMRs are visualized using TrkB(Nrtk2)tauEGFP knockin mice; and Aβ RA-LTMRs are labeled in Npy2r-GFP BAC transgenic mice (Li et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and references previous work (Li et al., 2011).

claim: Aδ-LTMRs are visualized using TrkB(Nrtk2)tauEGFP knockin mice.
source: We found that C-LTMRs can be visualized in ThCreER; Rosa26LSL-tdTomato mice treated with 4-HT; Aδ-LTMRs are visualized using TrkB(Nrtk2)tauEGFP knockin mice; and Aβ RA-LTMRs are labeled in Npy2r-GFP BAC transgenic mice (Li et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and references previous work (Li et al., 2011).

claim: Aβ RA-LTMRs are labeled in Npy2r-GFP BAC transgenic mice.
source: We found that C-LTMRs can be visualized in ThCreER; Rosa26LSL-tdTomato mice treated with 4-HT; Aδ-LTMRs are visualized using TrkB(Nrtk2)tauEGFP knockin mice; and Aβ RA-LTMRs are labeled in Npy2r-GFP BAC transgenic mice (Li et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and references previous work (Li et al., 2011).

claim: C-, Aδ-, and Aβ RA-LTMRs form morphologically similar longitudinal lanceolate endings associated with hair follicles in back hairy skin of the mouse.
source: Remarkably, in back hairy skin of the mouse, C-, Aδ-, and Aβ RA-LTMRs form morphologically similar longitudinal lanceolate endings associated with hair follicles (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunostaining images in Figure 1.

claim: Each type of LTMR lanceolate ending is associated with TSCs.
source: Immunostaining with S100, a glial cell marker, shows that each type of LTMR lanceolate ending is associated with TSCs, with cell bodies of TSCs residing at the base of lanceolate complexes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated by S100 immunostaining in Figure 1.

claim: Cell bodies of TSCs reside at the base of lanceolate complexes.
source: Immunostaining with S100, a glial cell marker, shows that each type of LTMR lanceolate ending is associated with TSCs, with cell bodies of TSCs residing at the base of lanceolate complexes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1.

claim: TSCs associated with C-, Aδ-, and Aβ RA-LTMRs exhibit extensive longitudinal processes extending toward the skin surface.
source: Moreover, TSCs associated with C-, Aδ-, and Aβ RA-LTMRs exhibit extensive longitudinal processes extending toward the skin surface.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1.

claim: TSC processes are parallel to the long axis of the hair follicle and encase individual longitudinal lanceolate endings of C-, Aδ-, and Aβ RA-LTMRs.
source: These finger-shaped processes are parallel to the long axis of the hair follicle and encase individual longitudinal lanceolate endings of C-, Aδ-, and Aβ RA-LTMRs (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Individual awl/auchene hair follicles have slightly more TSCs compared with zigzag hair follicles.
source: Quantification of TSCs associated with individual hair follicles shows that individual awl/auchene hair follicles have slightly more TSCs compared with zigzag hair follicles, and that guard hair follicles have many more TSCs than both zigzag and awl/auchene hairs (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and quantified in Figure 2C showing awl/auchene hairs have 5.0 ± 0.2 TSCs vs zigzag hairs with 3.7 ± 0.1 TSCs (p<0.001).

claim: Guard hair follicles have many more TSCs than both zigzag and awl/auchene hairs.
source: Quantification of TSCs associated with individual hair follicles shows that individual awl/auchene hair follicles have slightly more TSCs compared with zigzag hair follicles, and that guard hair follicles have many more TSCs than both zigzag and awl/auchene hairs (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and quantified in Figure 2C showing guard hairs have 13.4 ± 1.3 TSCs (p<0.001 compared to both other types).

claim: TSC densities for lanceolate complexes associated with zigzag and awl/auchene hair follicles are comparable.
source: Interestingly, TSC densities for lanceolate complexes associated with zigzag and awl/auchene hair follicles are comparable, while TSCs at guard hair follicles are considerably more compact (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and quantified in Figure 2D showing zigzag at 4.3 ± 0.1 TSCs/100 μm vs awl/auchene at 4.7 ± 0.2 TSCs/100 μm (p=0.084).

claim: TSCs at guard hair follicles are considerably more compact than those at zigzag and awl/auchene hair follicles.
source: Interestingly, TSC densities for lanceolate complexes associated with zigzag and awl/auchene hair follicles are comparable, while TSCs at guard hair follicles are considerably more compact (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and quantified in Figure 2D showing guard hairs at 7.7 ± 0.9 TSCs/100 μm (p<0.001 compared to both other types).

claim: The morphologies of individual TSCs associated with zigzag and awl/auchene hair follicles are comparable.
source: We found that the morphologies of individual TSCs associated with zigzag and awl/auchene hair follicles are comparable.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by measurements in Figure 2H-J showing no significant differences in cell body size, process width, or process length.

claim: TSCs at guard hair follicles have smaller cell bodies compared to those at zigzag and awl/auchene follicles.
source: In contrast, TSCs at guard hair follicles have smaller cell bodies, and fewer and considerably longer processes (Figure 2H–J).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and quantified in Figure 2H showing guard hair TSC cell bodies at 50.0 ± 3.5 μm2 (p<0.05 compared to zigzag or awl/auchene).

claim: TSCs at guard hair follicles have considerably longer processes compared to those at zigzag and awl/auchene follicles.
source: In contrast, TSCs at guard hair follicles have smaller cell bodies, and fewer and considerably longer processes (Figure 2H–J).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and quantified in Figure 2J showing guard hair TSC processes at 27.3 ± 1.1 μm (p<0.001 compared to zigzag or awl/auchene).

claim: Adjacent TSCs at individual hair follicles exhibit non-overlapping sets of processes.
source: In trunk hairy skin of Plp1CreER;Rosa26-Confetti animals, adjacent TSCs that are labeled by red and green fluorescence reporters exhibit non-overlapping sets of processes (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated by multicolor labeling in Figure 3A,B.

claim: C-LTMRs and Aδ-LTMRs form interdigitated lanceolate endings associated with processes belonging to the same TSC.
source: Interestingly, in back hairy skin sections from ThCreER;Rosa26tdTomato;TrkBtauEGFP mice, in which C-LTMRs, Aδ-LTMRs, and TSCs are visualized with tdTomato, GFP, and S100 immunostaining, respectively, we found that C-LTMRs and Aδ-LTMRs form interdigitated lanceolate endings associated with processes belonging to the same TSC (Figure 3C,C′).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated by triple labeling in Figure 3C,C′.

claim: Lanceolate complexes at all three hair follicle types appear as arrays of individual units composed of blade-shaped TSC processes and LTMR axonal endings aligned against the basal lamina of the hair follicle.
source: Transverse, ultrathin sections of lanceolate complexes associated with guard, awl/auchene, and zigzag hair follicles were collected, stained, and examined by electron microscopy (EM). Lanceolate complexes at all three hair follicle types appear as arrays of individual units composed of blade-shaped TSC processes and LTMR axonal endings aligned against the basal lamina of the hair follicle (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in EM images in Figure 4A.

claim: At guard hair follicles, each Aβ RA-LTMR lanceolate axonal terminal is encased by TSC processes on three sides.
source: At guard hair follicles, each Aβ RA-LTMR lanceolate axonal terminal (pseudo-colored in green) is encased by TSC processes (colored in pink) on three sides (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in EM images in Figure 4B.

claim: Cross sections of Aβ RA-LTMR lanceolate complexes at guard hairs appear triangular in shape.
source: Thus, cross sections of Aβ RA-LTMR lanceolate complexes appear triangular in shape.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in EM images in Figure 4B.

claim: At guard hair follicles, Aβ RA-LTMR axon terminals form small protrusions that are closely aligned, together with adjacent TSC processes, against the basal lamina of the hair follicle epithelial.
source: Interestingly, at the gaps or openings facing the hair follicle, the Aβ RA-LTMR axon terminals form small protrusions that are closely aligned, together with adjacent TSC processes, against the basal lamina of the hair follicle epithelial (Figure 4B,B′, arrows).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in EM images in Figure 4B,B′.

claim: The cytoplasm of Aβ RA-LTMR axons is densely packed with mitochondria.
source: Furthermore, the cytoplasm of Aβ RA-LTMR axons is densely packed with mitochondria.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in EM images in Figure 4B.

claim: At awl/auchene and zigzag hair follicles, axonal terminals are encased on two sides by TSC processes.
source: At awl/auchene and zigzag hair follicles, axonal terminals are encased on two sides by TSC processes, and thus cross sections of these lanceolate complexes appear spindle-shaped (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in EM images in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Cross sections of lanceolate complexes at awl/auchene and zigzag hair follicles appear spindle-shaped.
source: At awl/auchene and zigzag hair follicles, axonal terminals are encased on two sides by TSC processes, and thus cross sections of these lanceolate complexes appear spindle-shaped (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in EM images in Figure 4C,D.

claim: At awl/auchene and zigzag follicles, adjacent LTMR axonal endings often share the same TSC process.
source: Interestingly, at awl/auchene and zigzag follicles, adjacent LTMR axonal endings often share the same TSC process; this was rarely observed for Aβ RA-LTMR endings at guard hairs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in EM images in Figure 4C,D.

claim: The ultrastructural properties of lanceolate axons at awl/auchene and zigzag hair follicles are heterogeneous.
source: An additional, distinguishing feature of lanceolate complexes at awl/auchene and zigzag hair follicles, compared to those at guard hairs, is that the ultrastructural properties of the lanceolate axons are heterogeneous.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in EM images in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Some axons at awl/auchene and zigzag hair follicles contain many mitochondria, similar to the Aβ RA-LTMR endings at guard hair follicles, whereas others contain few mitochondria.
source: Indeed, some axons contain many mitochondria, similar to the Aβ RA-LTMR endings at guard hair follicles, whereas others contain few mitochondria (Figure 4C,D; Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in EM images in Figure 4C,D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Wnt1-Cre;TrkAf/f mice display a complete loss of C-LTMRs.
source: We found that Wnt1-Cre;TrkAf/f mice, in which the nerve growth factor (NGF) receptor gene TrkA (Nrtk1) is selectively ablated in DRG neurons and other cells of neural crest origin, display a complete loss of C-LTMRs (Figure 6A,A′).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown by TH immunostaining in Figure 6A,A′.

claim: Lanceolate endings of Aβ RA-LTMRs at awl/auchene and guard hair follicles are missing in Wnt1-Cre;TrkAf/f mice.
source: Unexpectedly, lanceolate endings of Aβ RA-LTMRs at awl/auchene and guard hair follicles are also missing in Wnt1-Cre;TrkAf/f mice (Figure 6B,B′), although Aβ RA-LTMR neurons labeled by Npy2r-GFP are still present in DRGs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown by GFP immunostaining in Figure 6B,B′.

claim: C-LTMR and Aβ RA-LTMR endings in the skin are dependent on NGF–TrkA signaling for development.
source: Thus, C-LTMR and Aβ RA-LTMR endings in the skin are dependent on NGF–TrkA signaling for development.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the Results section based on the loss of these endings in TrkA mutants.

claim: The axonal endings of Aδ-LTMRs at both awl/auchene and zigzag hair follicles remain intact in Wnt1-Cre;TrkAf/f mice.
source: In contrast, the axonal endings of Aδ-LTMRs at both awl/auchene and zigzag hair follicles remain intact in these mutant mice (Figure 6C,C′).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown by GFP immunostaining in Figure 6C,C′.

claim: The lanceolate endings with few mitochondria belong to C-LTMRs while those with abundant mitochondria belong to Aδ-LTMRs or Aβ RA-LTMRs.
source: Assuming that the TrkA mutation has no effect on mitochondria density in Aδ-LTMR axonal terminals, this finding indicates that the lanceolate endings with few mitochondria belong to C-LTMRs while those with abundant mitochondria belong to Aδ-LTMRs or Aβ RA-LTMRs (Figure 5; Figure 6F–H).
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the Results section based on the differential loss of axon types in TrkA mutants and their mitochondrial content.

claim: Numerous small vesicles are located within the cytoplasm of lanceolate endings of all LTMR subtypes.
source: Several additional interesting ultrastructural features of LTMR lanceolate complexes at all three hair follicle subtypes were observed. In particular, numerous small vesicles are located within the cytoplasm of lanceolate endings of all LTMR subtypes (Figure 7A–C, arrows).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in EM images in Figure 7A-C.

claim: These vesicles are glutamate-containing vesicles, which may mediate communication with TSCs and thereby regulate lanceolate complex assembly and maintenance.
source: Recent studies suggest that these are glutamate-containing vesicles, which may mediate communication with TSCs and thereby regulate lanceolate complex assembly and maintenance (Woo et al., 2012; Banks et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to recent studies (Woo et al., 2012; Banks et al., 2013).

claim: Many pinocytotic vesicles are associated with both the inner and outer surfaces of TSC processes.
source: Additionally, many pinocytotic vesicles are associated with both the inner and outer surfaces of TSC processes (Figure 7A–C, arrowheads).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in EM images in Figure 7A-C.

claim: There is an abundance of prominent hemidesmosomes located along the outer membranes of the outer root sheath epithelial cells of the three hair follicle subtypes.
source: Intriguingly, there is an abundance of prominent hemidesmosomes located along the outer membranes of the outer root sheath epithelial cells of the three hair follicle subtypes (Figure 7D–G, white arrow heads).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in EM images in Figure 7D-G.

claim: Fine filament-like structures emanate from hemidesmosomes, pass through the basal lamina, and appear to form direct contacts with the membranes of Aβ RA-LTMR, Aδ-LTMR, and C-LTMR lanceolate axonal endings as well as TSC processes.
source: Fine filament-like structures emanate from these hemidesmosomes, pass through the basal lamina, and appear to form direct contacts with the membranes of Aβ RA-LTMR, Aδ-LTMR, and C-LTMR lanceolate axonal endings as well as TSC processes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in EM images in Figure 7D-G.

claim: These tether-like filaments are approximately 100 nm in length.
source: These tether-like filaments are approximately 100 nm in length and may be similar to anchoring filaments or anchoring fibrils, which are essential components of dermo–epidermal junctions connecting basal keratinocytes with dermal cell types (Keene et al., 1987; Regauer et al., 1990; Burgeson and Christiano, 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on EM measurements.

claim: 100% of the hair follicles lacking TSCs exhibited a complete loss of longitudinal lanceolate endings.
source: Remarkably, 100% of the hair follicles lacking TSCs exhibited a complete loss of longitudinal lanceolate endings and a partial loss of circumferential endings labeled by Tuj1 and NFH immunostaining (Figure 8A,A′,B,B′).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown by immunostaining in Figure 8A,A′,B,B′.

claim: Hair follicles lacking TSCs exhibited a partial loss of circumferential endings labeled by Tuj1 and NFH immunostaining.
source: Remarkably, 100% of the hair follicles lacking TSCs exhibited a complete loss of longitudinal lanceolate endings and a partial loss of circumferential endings labeled by Tuj1 and NFH immunostaining (Figure 8A,A′,B,B′).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown by immunostaining in Figure 8A,A′,B,B′.

claim: A partial loss of CGRP+ circumferential endings was observed in hair follicles lacking TSCs.
source: A partial loss of CGRP+ circumferential endings was also observed (Figure 8C,C′).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown by immunostaining in Figure 8C,C′.

claim: LTMR axon terminals retract from hair follicles following ablation of TSCs.
source: These findings indicate that LTMR axon terminals retract from hair follicles following ablation of TSCs.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the Results section based on the loss of LTMR endings after TSC ablation.

claim: TSCs remain intact and in close association with hair follicles in the absence of LTMR endings.
source: Strikingly, TSCs, labeled by S100 immunostaining, remained intact and in close association with hair follicles in the absence of LTMR endings (Figure 9B,B′).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown by S100 immunostaining in Figure 9B,B′.

claim: Even 44 days following skin denervation, TSCs at denervated hair follicles remained intact.
source: Even 44 days following skin denervation, TSCs at denervated hair follicles remained intact (Figure 9C,C′,D,D′,E,E′).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown by immunostaining in Figure 9C,C′,D,D′,E,E′.

claim: Both Schwann cells associated with circumferential axonal terminals at hair follicles and myelinating Schwann cells in the dermis had degenerated in the absence of cutaneous nerves.
source: In contrast, both Schwann cells associated with circumferential axonal terminals at hair follicles (Figure 9D,D′; white arrow) and myelinating Schwann cells in the dermis, visualized by S100 and MBP immunostaining (Figure 9E,E′), had degenerated in the absence of cutaneous nerves.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown by immunostaining in Figure 9D,D′,E,E′.

claim: Comparable numbers of TSCs were present at hair follicles on control and denervated sides 5 weeks following skin denervation.
source: This quantitative assessment revealed that, despite complete loss of cutaneous LTMR endings on the denervated side of the animal, comparable numbers of TSCs were present at hair follicles on control and denervated sides (Figure 9G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and quantified in Figure 9G.

claim: TSCs associated with Aβ RA-LTMRs, Aδ-LTMRs, and C-LTMRs maintain both their location and structural integrity in the absence of axonal processes in adult mice, for at least several weeks.
source: Therefore, TSCs associated with Aβ RA-LTMRs, Aδ-LTMRs, and C-LTMRs, maintain both their location and structural integrity in the absence of axonal processes in adult mice, for at least several weeks.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the denervation experiments.

claim: By 33 days after denervation, approximately 70% of the denervated skin had been innervated.
source: In contrast to 7 days after denervation, where few fibers were seen in the denervated skin, by 33 days after denervation, approximately 70% of the denervated skin had been innervated (Figure 10A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown by immunostaining in Figure 10A,B.

claim: The majority of re-innervation most likely derives from axons that had regenerated from the severed dorsal cutaneous nerves.
source: The majority of re-innervation most likely derives from axons that had regenerated from the severed dorsal cutaneous nerves (Jackson and Diamond, 1984).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to previous work (Jackson and Diamond, 1984).

claim: Approximately 90% of hair follicles exhibited at least some re-innervation by 5 weeks after denervation.
source: Overall, approximately 90% of hair follicles exhibited at least some re-innervation by 5 weeks after denervation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on observations from Figure 10.

claim: Lanceolate complexes at guard hairs have considerably more advanced recovery compared to non-guard hair follicles.
source: Lanceolate complexes at guard hairs have considerably more advanced recovery compared to non-guard hair follicles.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on observations from Figure 10.

claim: 83 days following denervation, Npy2r-GFP+ axons had re-innervated awl/auchene and guard hair follicles in the denervated skin region.
source: Remarkably, 83 days following denervation, Npy2r-GFP+ axons had re-innervated awl/auchene and guard hair follicles in the denervated skin region (Figure 10H, white arrowheads).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown by GFP immunostaining in Figure 10H.

claim: The majority of GFP+ axons had developed typical longitudinal lanceolate endings associated with the denervated guard and awl/auchene hairs.
source: While some of the Aβ RA-LTMR axon terminals exhibited simple circumferential endings around hair follicles at this time point and excess sprouting of GFP+ axons innervating adjacent zigzag hair follicles was occasionally seen, the majority of GFP+ axons had developed typical longitudinal lanceolate endings associated with the denervated guard and awl/auchene hairs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on observations from Figure 10H.

claim: The specificity of the LTMR subtype/hair follicle relationship is largely if not completely preserved, at least for Aβ RA-LTMRs, following re-innervation.
source: Furthermore, these intact TSCs become re-associated with the lanceolate endings of regenerated LTMRs, and the specificity of the LTMR subtype/hair follicle relationship is largely if not completely preserved, at least for Aβ RA-LTMRs, following re-innervation.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the re-innervation experiments with Npy2r-GFP mice.

claim: The unique physiological properties and adaptation rates of Aβ RA-, Aδ-, and C-LTMRs associated with awl/auchene and zigzag hair follicles are due to intrinsic neuronal differences rather than unique end organ cell types or morphologies.
source: These findings provide strong support for a model, in which the unique physiological properties and adaptation rates of Aβ RA-, Aδ-, and C-LTMRs associated with awl/auchene and zigzag hair follicles are due to intrinsic neuronal differences rather than unique end organ cell types or morphologies.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the Discussion section based on the findings that different LTMR subtypes share similar morphologies and TSCs.

claim: TSCs serve as anchors or scaffolds that maintain LTMR endings and lanceolate complex structure and integrity.
source: Nevertheless, our findings indicate that TSCs serve as anchors or scaffolds that maintain LTMR endings and lanceolate complex structure and integrity, whereas LTMR axonal endings of adult mice are not required for maintenance of TSCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion section based on the ablation and denervation experiments.
